q.q: A friend asks you what 'artificial intelligence' means. Which answer is best?
o: Computer systems that do tasks normally needing human intelligence
A robot that has its own thoughts, feelings and wishes
Any computer system that runs a program written by a person
A very fast calculator that always gives the right answer
q.why: AI recognises, predicts, decides and produces language; it does not have feelings.

q.q: Which of these everyday features most needs AI to work?
o: A light switch
A digital clock
A microwave timer
Face unlock on a phone
q.why: Face unlock must recognise your face in new situations.

q.q: In most modern AI systems, how are the rules for making decisions created?
o: They are copied from older AI systems
The computer learns them from patterns in data
The user enters them each time the AI is used
A programmer types in every single rule
q.why: Modern AI works out its own rules from examples.

q.q: How is a traditional program different from a machine learning AI system?
o: A traditional program can guess about new situations
A traditional program's answers are based on probability
In a traditional program a person writes every rule
A traditional program learns rules from examples
q.why: A calculator follows rules a programmer wrote; AI learns rules from examples.

q.q: Why can an AI system give a wrong answer even if the programmer made no mistakes?
o: Its guesses are based on probability
It cannot handle any data it has seen before
It only does exactly what it was told
It deliberately chooses wrong answers sometimes
q.why: AI makes a best guess from patterns, so it can be wrong.

q.q: A chatbot writes "I'm so excited to help!" What does this tell you?
o: The words fit the conversation, but it does not feel anything
The chatbot has real feelings, just like a person does
The chatbot's training data must have been faulty
The chatbot has become conscious and can now think
q.why: Fluent language is not the same as real feelings or understanding.

q.q: Which statement about AI is true?
o: Every robot used in a factory relies on AI
AI can only run on enormous supercomputers
Most AI is software running on phones, laptops and servers
All AI is built into robots that can move around
q.why: Most AI is software, and many factory robots have no AI at all.

q.q: What is AI actually made of, according to the notes?
o: Maths and statistics running on powerful computers
Magic that even experts cannot explain
A list of rules written by film makers
Living brain cells grown in a laboratory
q.why: AI is not magic: it is maths and statistics.

q.q: An app predicts how long your journey will take. Which type of AI task is this?
o: Producing language
Making predictions
Recognising things
Making decisions about chess moves
q.why: Working out a journey time is a prediction.

q.q: What is an algorithm?
o: A set of step-by-step instructions
A robot that follows commands
A collection of raw facts and figures
A type of computer screen
q.why: All programs, including AI, follow an algorithm.

q.q: In the Turing test, what is the judge trying to decide?
o: How fast the computer does sums
How much memory the computer has
Which hidden partner is the computer
Whether the computer can win at chess
q.why: A judge tries to tell which hidden partner is the computer.

q.q: What did Alan Turing call the game that is now known as the Turing test?
o: The Dartmouth challenge
The Enigma test
The imitation game
The thinking game
q.why: Turing suggested the 'imitation game' in his 1950 paper.

q.q: In which year did Turing write his famous paper asking 'Can machines think?'
q.why: Turing's paper and the Turing test date from 1950.

q.q: During the Second World War, Alan Turing helped break German codes at which place?
o: DeepMind in London
IBM in the USA
Dartmouth
Bletchley Park
q.why: He helped break German codes at Bletchley Park.

q.q: When was the term 'artificial intelligence' used for a meeting of scientists, making AI a field of study?
o: 1950, in Turing's paper
1997, when Deep Blue won
1956, at the Dartmouth workshop
1966, when ELIZA was made
q.why: John McCarthy coined the term for the 1956 Dartmouth workshop.

q.q: What was ELIZA (1966)?
o: The first computer to beat a chess champion
An AI that predicted the shapes of proteins
One of the first chatbots, which followed simple rules
The first voice assistant on a phone
q.why: ELIZA replied like a counsellor using simple rules.

q.q: IBM's Deep Blue beat world chess champion Garry Kasparov in which year?
q.why: IBM's Deep Blue won the six-game match in 1997.

q.q: How did Deep Blue mainly work?
o: Predicting the next word in a conversation
Brute force search and rules written by experts
Copying the moves of Lee Sedol
Machine learning from millions of self-played games
q.why: It searched around 200 million positions per second using hand-written rules.

q.q: Why was AlphaGo's win in 2016 seen as a big step forward?
o: Go is a much simpler game than chess, so it was easier
It was the first AI ever built in the United Kingdom
It searched far more positions per second than Deep Blue
It learned strategies by machine learning, in a far more complex game
q.why: AlphaGo learned by studying games and playing itself, in a game far more complex than chess.

q.q: What did DeepMind's AlphaFold do?
o: Beat the world champion at Go
Recognised faces to unlock phones
Wrote fluent text for millions of users
Predicted the 3D shapes of proteins
q.why: AlphaFold helped medical research; its creators shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

q.q: Why do many experts say the Turing test is not a good measure of intelligence?
o: It only measures how quickly a computer can do sums
Chatbots can fool people in short chats yet still make basic mistakes
It can only be carried out on very old computers
No computer has ever passed even a very short conversation
q.why: Fooling people briefly does not mean understanding the world.

q.q: What is narrow AI?
o: AI that is not very good at any task it is given
AI that can only run on small devices like phones
AI that can learn and do any intellectual task a human can
AI designed to do one specific task or a small set of related tasks
q.why: Narrow AI can be extremely good at one task but cannot transfer its skill.

q.q: Which of these systems is narrow AI?
o: A machine that understands everything
A robot that can do any job a human can
A computer that feels emotions
A spam filter
q.why: A spam filter does one specific task.

q.q: Which statement about general AI today is correct?
o: It is built into every smartphone
It was invented in 1956
It exists, but only in laboratories
It does not exist yet
q.why: All AI today is narrow AI.

q.q: What is another name for general AI?
o: Deep learning
AGI
Narrow AI
Weak AI
q.why: Narrow AI is also called weak AI; general AI is AGI.

q.q: A chess program beats grandmasters but cannot answer a Geography question. This shows it is...
o: narrow AI
general AI
broken
not using machine learning
q.why: It can only do the task it was built for.

q.q: What would general AI be able to do?
o: Sort emails into spam and not spam
Search 200 million chess positions a second
Do one task better than any human
Learn and carry out any intellectual task a human can
q.why: General AI could switch between tasks and genuinely understand them.

q.q: Chatbots can talk about almost any subject. Why are they still described as narrow?
o: They can only discuss one subject at a time with each user
They can only be used by one person at a time in a school
They were built before general AI had been fully invented
They are trained to produce likely text and do not reliably reason
q.why: They seem general but cannot reliably reason, plan or understand the world.

q.q: A headline says 'General AI has arrived!' What does the page suggest?
o: Believe it, because general AI was completed in 2022
Believe it, as long as the article mentions chatbots
Ignore it, because AI of any kind does not really exist
Be cautious: experts disagree about whether or when it will be built
q.why: General AI does not exist yet, and experts strongly disagree about it.

q.q: Which is narrow AI also called?
o: AGI
Weak AI
General AI
Strong AI
q.why: Narrow AI is also called weak AI.

q.q: What job does the recommendation system in a video app do?
o: Blocks every advert that is shown on a website
Predicts what you might want to watch, listen to or buy next
Checks whether your face matches the owner's face
Turns your spoken words into text for an app
q.why: It uses patterns in your and other users' data.

q.q: A smart speaker uses speech recognition. What does speech recognition do?
o: Guessing the next word you are going to type
Turning written text into a spoken voice
Recognising people's faces in photos
Turning spoken words into text the computer can use
q.why: Voice assistants use it to understand what you say.

q.q: What data is a spam filter trained on?
o: Emails that people have marked as spam or not spam
Thousands of hours of recorded speech
Millions of labelled photos of faces
Live traffic data from millions of phones
q.why: Labelled emails teach it what spam looks like.

q.q: Which everyday AI predicts how long a journey will take?
o: A spam filter
Autocorrect
Face unlock
A maps app
q.why: It uses live and past traffic data.

q.q: What does facial recognition in face unlock do?
o: Checks whether the face in front of the camera matches the owner's
Groups all of your photos by the people that appear in them
Changes a person's face in a video to make a deepfake
Finds pictures of dogs and beaches in your photo library
q.why: Face unlock matches your face to the owner's.

q.q: What pattern does a recommendation system look for?
o: Videos that are the shortest in length on the whole site
Videos that were uploaded most recently by anyone at all
People who watched the same videos as you also watched this one
Videos that have no adverts shown before or during them
q.why: It compares your history with similar users.

q.q: Why do recommendations become more personal the more you use an app?
o: The app's AI becomes general AI
The app has more data about you
The app stops using patterns
The app deletes other users' data
q.why: More data about you means more personal suggestions.

q.q: What is a filter bubble?
o: A setting that blocks every recommendation
A folder that spam emails are moved into
Only seeing more and more of the same kind of thing
A fault that stops videos loading properly
q.why: Recommendation systems keep you watching, which can narrow what you see.

q.q: Which use of AI happens behind the scenes rather than on your own device?
o: A voice assistant answering a question you asked it
Predictive text guessing the next word you will type
A bank spotting unusual card payments that might be fraud
Face unlock opening your phone when it sees you
q.why: Banks use AI to spot possible fraud; you never see it directly.

q.q: Which answer would gain full marks for 'Describe one use of AI'?
o: Spam filters, sat navs and face unlock all use AI in different ways.
A spam filter uses AI to predict whether an email is spam and moves it to a junk folder.
A spam filter is a type of artificial intelligence that you find on email.
AI is used in email to make the email system work better for users.
q.why: An exam answer should give the use and say what the AI does.

q.q: What data does predictive text learn from?
o: Millions of labelled photos
The owner's face
Huge amounts of written text, plus what you usually type
Live traffic data from millions of phones
q.why: Predictive text guesses the next word from text patterns.

q.q: What is machine learning?
o: A way of teaching people how to use computers and apps
A type of AI where a computer learns from examples, not written rules
A type of program where a programmer writes every single rule
A robot that teaches itself to walk without any software
q.why: Machine learning finds patterns in data to make predictions.

q.q: In machine learning, each training photo is given a 'label'. What is it?
o: A feature the model looks at
The name given to the finished model
The percentage of examples the model gets right
The correct answer attached to a training example
q.why: E.g. each photo is labelled cat or dog.

q.q: Training on data produces something that makes predictions. What is it called?
o: A label
A model
A feature
A prompt
q.why: The model is what makes predictions.

q.q: Which is the correct order of the machine learning process?
o: Label, collect, test, train, use
Collect, label, train, test, use
Collect, train, label, test, use
Collect, label, test, train, use
q.why: Remember C-L-T-T-U.

q.q: Why should a model never be tested on the same examples it learned from?
o: To check the model works on examples it has never seen
Testing data must not have labels
Training data cannot be stored after it is used
So the model can learn more during testing
q.why: Otherwise a high score proves nothing, like seeing the exam questions the day before.

q.q: Why is it hard to write rules by hand for a spam filter?
o: Spam emails never contain any words
Computers cannot read the text of emails
There are only three types of spam
Spam is too varied, and spammers change tactics
q.why: A machine learning filter can be retrained on new examples instead.

q.q: For an email, which of these is a feature?
o: The accuracy of the model
The number of links in the email
The set of testing emails
The label 'spam' given to it
q.why: Features are the details a model uses to decide.

q.q: What is a neural network?
o: A long list of hand-written rules for sorting emails
A network of computers joined together with cables and Wi-Fi
A real human brain that has been connected to a computer
A model loosely inspired by the brain, made of layers of connected units
q.why: Connections are adjusted during training until answers are right.

q.q: What is a neural network with many layers called?
o: Deep learning
A classifier
General AI
Narrow learning
q.why: Many layers = deep learning.

q.q: What happens during training of a neural network?
o: The labels are removed from the data
The strength of each connection is adjusted bit by bit
A programmer writes a rule for each connection
New layers are added for each example
q.why: Connections are adjusted until the network gives the right answers.

q.q: A model performs badly after testing. What should happen next?
o: Use it for real anyway
Remove all the labels
Collect more or better data and train again
Test it on the training data instead
q.why: If it is not accurate enough, improve the data and retrain.

q.q: What is a classifier?
o: A list of all the features that appear in a photo
A person whose job is to label all the training data
A model that sorts each input into one of a fixed set of groups
A model that creates new text, images or music from a prompt
q.why: E.g. cat or dog, spam or not spam.

q.q: What are the groups a classifier sorts inputs into called?
o: Features
Classes
Labels
Layers
q.why: A spam filter has two classes: spam and not spam.

q.q: A classifier gets 45 out of 50 test photos right. What is its accuracy?
A model classifies 180 of 200 test photos correctly. What is its accuracy?
A spam filter gets 72 out of 80 test emails right. What is its accuracy?
A model is 90% accurate. About how many examples in every 10 will it get wrong?
q.why: Accuracy is never a guarantee; 90% means about 1 in 10 wrong.

q.q: The cat/dog model gets most night-time photos wrong. What is the most likely reason?
o: The wildlife camera stopped working properly at night
Cats and dogs have exactly the same features at night
There were very few night-time photos in the training data
Accuracy cannot be measured for photos taken at night
q.why: A model is poor at things missing from its training data.

q.q: The cat/dog classifier was shown a fox and said 'dog'. Why?
o: It only had two classes, so it had to choose cat or dog
It had been trained on lots of fox photos
The fox photo was labelled 'dog'
Foxes and dogs have exactly the same features
q.why: A classifier must pick one of its fixed classes.

q.q: Which change is most likely to improve the classifier?
o: Test it on the training photos
Use fewer training photos
Remove the labels from the photos
Add more varied training photos
q.why: More, and more varied, data usually helps.

q.q: Why should a human check an AI's decision in medicine even if it is 90% accurate?
o: 90% accuracy means the AI will always be right for patients
AI cannot be trained on photos of hospital scans
Doctors are not allowed to use computers to help them
It will still get some cases wrong, and the decision is important
q.why: Even an accurate model makes mistakes.

q.q: How does generative AI differ from AI such as a spam filter?
o: It creates new content
It never uses any data
It only sorts things into groups
It only works offline
q.why: A spam filter sorts; generative AI generates.

q.q: At its simplest, what does a large language model do?
o: Predicts the next word, again and again
Searches a list of rules written by experts
Copies whole web pages into its reply
Looks up each answer in a dictionary
q.why: It builds text one likely word at a time.

q.q: When using a chatbot, what is meant by a 'prompt'?
o: The instruction or question you give an AI tool
A rating given to the AI during fine-tuning
The reply that the AI writes back
The data the AI was trained on
q.why: The model replies to your prompt.

q.q: Why is a large language model called 'large'?
o: It can only be run in a large room of computers
It needs a very large screen to display its answers
It is a huge neural network trained on an enormous amount of text
It always writes very long answers
q.why: It is trained on far more text than any human could read.

q.q: Strictly speaking, what do LLMs predict?
o: Pictures that match the words
Whole sentences at a time
Single letters only
Tokens: words or parts of words
q.why: Next word is a good way to picture it, but strictly they predict tokens.

q.q: What happens during fine-tuning of a chatbot?
o: It predicts the reply to your prompt
It is tested on photos of cats and dogs
People rate and correct its answers to make it more helpful
It reads huge amounts of text for the first time
q.why: Fine-tuning comes after pre-training and uses human feedback.

q.q: During which stage does an LLM pick up grammar, facts and styles of writing?
o: Answering your prompt
Pre-training
Fine-tuning
Testing
q.why: Pre-training on huge amounts of text teaches it to predict the next word.

q.q: Why can an LLM give a confident answer that is wrong?
o: It has run out of training data to use
It always lies to users on purpose
It predicts likely words, not checked facts
Someone has hacked into the model
q.why: Likely is not the same as true.

q.q: Why might an LLM not know about a news story from last week?
o: It may only know what was in its training text, unless it can search
News stories are always filtered out during fine-tuning
LLMs cannot read any text that is written in English
LLMs are only allowed to discuss events from many years ago
q.why: Recent events may not be in its training data.

q.q: Which everyday tool does a very small version of what an LLM does?
o: Face unlock on a phone
A sat nav in a car
A pocket calculator
Predictive text on your phone
q.why: Predictive text guesses the next word.

q.q: What does it mean when an AI tool 'hallucinates'?
o: When AI is unfair to certain groups of people
When a computer overheats and then crashes
When AI makes up false information that sounds true
When AI refuses to answer any question
q.why: It sounds confident but is wrong; unfairness is bias.

q.q: What is the most common cause of bias in an AI system?
o: The speed of the internet connection
Unbalanced or unfair training data
The programmer writing unfair rules by hand
The AI choosing to be unfair on purpose
q.why: Bias in, bias out.

q.q: A chatbot gives you a quote from a famous scientist for your project. What should you do?
o: Use it straight away
Check it in a reliable source first
Change a few words and then use it
Ask the chatbot if it is sure, then use it
q.why: The chatbot could have made it up; asking it again is not real checking.

q.q: Which is the best way to reduce bias in an AI system?
o: Train it on more balanced data and test results for different groups
Let it make all of its decisions without any people
Hide how the system works from the people who use it
Use less data so that it learns fewer patterns overall
q.why: Balanced data, testing and human oversight all help.

q.q: A recruitment AI marked down CVs that included the word "women's". Why?
o: It had been hacked by another company
It was programmed to dislike chess clubs
It could not read the apostrophe in "women's"
It learned from past CVs that mostly came from men
q.why: It learned to prefer male applicants from unbalanced data.

q.q: The Gender Shades study found some face-analysis systems were least accurate for which group?
o: Lighter-skinned men
Older men
Lighter-skinned women
Darker-skinned women
q.why: Training photos had far more lighter-skinned faces, especially men's.

q.q: What does 'black box' mean as a limitation of AI?
o: It is often hard to explain why the AI made a decision
The AI cannot display any colours on screen
The AI only works properly in a dark room
The AI's answers are always hidden from users
q.why: With large neural networks the reasoning is hard to see.

q.q: An AI labels a picture of a muffin as a dog. Which limitation does this show?
o: Energy use
Black box
No common sense
Hallucinating a source
q.why: AI can make mistakes no person would make.

q.q: What environmental cost do large AI models have?
o: They use a lot of electricity, and water for cooling
They need new phones every month
They produce large amounts of paper waste
They use up the storage on your phone
q.why: Data centres use electricity and water.

q.q: What is ethics about?
o: Making AI tools run faster
Collecting lots of training data
Deciding what is right and wrong
Writing clear prompts for AI
q.why: Just because AI can do something does not mean it should.

q.q: Which is an honest use of AI for homework, if your teacher allows it?
o: Getting it to answer your online test for you
Asking it to write your essay, then handing it in
Asking it to explain a topic, then writing notes in your own words
Changing a few words in an AI essay so it looks like yours
q.why: You do the thinking and the writing.

q.q: Handing in AI-written work as your own is a form of...
o: plagiarism
a deepfake
citation
fine-tuning
q.why: Plagiarism is presenting someone else's work as yours.

q.q: How do exam boards treat submitting AI-generated coursework as your own?
o: As fine, as long as you change some of the words first
As a small mistake, like a spelling error in an essay
As acceptable, as long as all of the work is accurate
As malpractice, which can lead to losing marks or disqualification
q.why: Always follow your school's rules on AI.

q.q: Which of these should you keep out of an AI chatbot?
o: A spelling question
Your home address and password
A request for revision tips
A question about volcanoes
q.why: Protect your personal data.

q.q: Which of these is a deepfake?
o: A video file that has become corrupted
An AI-made fake image, video or audio of a real person
A real photo that has been cropped smaller
A real video that has gone viral online
q.why: It shows someone saying or doing something they never did.

q.q: Which is an example of a deepfake being used to scam people?
o: A cloned voice of a family member asking for money
A recommendation for a new video you might enjoy
A chatbot explaining photosynthesis in simple words
A spam filter moving an email into the junk folder
q.why: Cloned voices are a deepfake scam.

q.q: Which is the best way to check whether a video might be a deepfake?
o: Look for odd details and check whether trusted news sources report it
Check how many times it has been shared and liked online
See whether it has a catchy title and an exciting thumbnail
Watch it again at a higher volume to hear it more clearly
q.why: Odd hands, teeth, edges and lighting, plus trusted sources, help spot fakes.

q.q: What is the most likely effect of AI on jobs?
o: Only jobs in computing will be affected, and all other jobs will stay the same
Every job will disappear within a few years as AI takes over all work
Some tasks will be automated, many jobs will change and new ones will appear
Nothing at all will change about jobs, because AI is just a passing fad
q.why: A balanced view: change, not simply loss.

q.q: Why should you check the minimum age before using an AI tool?
o: AI tools only recognise adults' voices and faces
Younger users are always given less accurate answers
Many AI tools have a minimum age, often 13 and sometimes 18
The tool deletes every account after one year of use
q.why: Use only tools your school or parents allow.

q.q: Which is the best prompt?
o: Tell me everything you know about volcanoes.
Explain volcanoes to me like a university professor.
Volcanoes, explain, bullet points, Geography, now.
I'm in Year 9. Explain how volcanoes form in 5 short bullet points.
q.why: It gives context, a task and a format.

q.q: 'Use 5 bullet points with simple words' is which part of a good prompt?
o: Role or context
Format
Limits
Task
q.why: Format is how you want the answer laid out.

q.q: 'I'm a Year 9 pupil revising for a Geography test' is which part of a good prompt?
o: Limits
Context
Task
Format
q.why: It says who you are and what you need it for.

q.q: What should you do if the AI's first answer is too complicated?
o: Stop using AI for that topic altogether
Copy the complicated answer anyway
Refine the prompt, e.g. ask for simpler words
Type exactly the same prompt in again
q.why: Refining prompts gets better answers.

q.q: An AI tool gives you a website link as a source. What should you do?
o: Copy it straight into your bibliography as it is
Leave the link out but keep the fact it supported
Ask the AI to promise you that the link is real
Open it to check it exists and says what the AI claims
q.why: AI can hallucinate links.

q.q: Your teacher allows AI for a task. What should you write down to cite your AI use?
o: Your password and login details
The tool, the date and the prompts you used
Only the name of the AI company
The exact time the AI took to reply
q.why: This shows honestly how you used it.

q.q: Two sources disagree about a fact the AI gave you. What do the notes suggest?
o: Use whichever source is shorter
Leave the fact out of all your work
Ask a teacher
Use the fact the AI gave
q.why: Ask a teacher if two sources disagree.

q.q: What does 'think of AI as a study partner, not a ghostwriter' mean?
o: AI should support your thinking, not do your work for you
AI should only be used at night
AI should be kept secret from your teacher
AI should write your work but not your notes
q.why: If you could not explain your work without the AI, you let it do too much.

q.q: Which is a reliable source for checking a fact given by an AI tool?
o: A comment on social media
The same AI tool asked twice
BBC Bitesize
Another AI chatbot
q.why: The notes list textbooks, class notes, BBC Bitesize and official websites.
